html:
Jodensavanne, the Jewish Savanna, was a settlement of Sephardic Jewish planters on the Suriname River, built from the 1650s. Its synagogue, finished in 1685, was among the first large synagogues in the Americas.

Jews of Portuguese and Spanish descent, many from Dutch Brazil, came to Suriname under the English and stayed under the Dutch. They were granted unusual rights to own land and run their own affairs. Their sugar plantations, like all others in the colony, were worked by enslaved Africans.

The settlement declined as planters moved to Paramaribo, and a fire in 1832 left it in ruins. The site now has the remains of the synagogue and its cemeteries. It belongs to the story of the Sephardic diaspora that runs from Iberia through Dutch Brazil to the Dutch Caribbean.
